title: Pixel-style bonded sense amps on every 256-cell bitline
idea: Scale jump from stacked CMOS image sensors (one bonded readout per pixel) to DRAM: hybrid-bond the array wafer to a 28 nm periphery wafer at 0.5 um pitch so every ~9 um (256-cell) bitline gets its own sense amp directly beneath it, instead of 1024-cell bitlines ending in edge SA stripes. The array die becomes pure cells; SAs, sub-wordline drivers and decoders all sit on the cheap wafer below.
why: Cbl drops ~3-4x so Cs can fall from ~5 fF to ~1.5-2 fF (capacitor AR ~60:1 -> ~25:1, fact 1), and the ~49% periphery leaves the expensive array die (fact 7); est. 25-35% lower cost per bit.

title: Roving sense amp visits sampled bitlines in picosecond turns
idea: Time jump inside one row cycle: each bitline gets a tiny isolation switch that freezes its charge-shared signal, then one fast SA on a ~100 ps cycle visits 8 bitlines in turn, resolving and writing back each, like the column-shared ADCs of image sensors. SA count falls 8x for ~4 ns of added serial latency per segment.
why: SA stripes are a large slice of the ~49% periphery (fact 7); 8x fewer SAs cuts SA-stripe area ~60-70% net of switches, roughly 8-12% of die area.

title: Frequency-tuned resonators select mats instead of decoder wiring
idea: Shift the address from space to frequency: each mat's local wordline-driver enable is gated by a micron-scale AlN film-bulk acoustic resonator tuned to a unique GHz tone, and one shared RF line selects a mat by broadcasting its tone; only a short local decoder picks the row inside the mat. Predecoders and the global address bus collapse into one line plus a frequency synthesizer.
why: Attacks decoder and global-routing periphery (fact 7) and address-bus wire energy; est. 3-6% die area saved and fewer routing metal layers.

title: Stepwise adiabatic wordline charging from a tank-capacitor ladder
idea: Time-stretch the wordline edge from ~1 ns to ~5 ns and charge it in 6 voltage steps from a ladder of deep-trench tank capacitors on the periphery wafer that recapture the charge when the wordline falls, so each 3 V wordline is charged quasi-adiabatically instead of straight from the VPP pump.
why: Wordline CV^2 at ~3 V plus ~30-40%-efficient pumps are stuck at the voltage floor (fact 10); stepwise charging cuts wordline+pump energy ~4-5x, about 10-15% of activation energy, for a few ns of tRCD.

title: 3D-NAND-like vertical CCD strings as capacitor-less DRAM
idea: Scale-and-time jump back to 1970s CCD memory, rebuilt as a 3D-NAND-style vertical string: each of 100+ stacked gate tiers holds a charge packet in an IGZO channel potential well, and a read clocks packets down the string (~10 ns per tier) into one floating-diffusion sense node at the bottom, then recirculates them to the top. No per-tier capacitor or lateral transistor exists; there is one sense amp per string.
why: Bypasses both 3D DRAM blockers, the capacitor and the lateral transistor (fact 2), and amortizes periphery over 100 tiers (fact 7); 5-10x the density of 6F2 if charge-transfer efficiency stays >0.9999, with wide-gap IGZO keeping dark current low.

title: Compressed-sensing reads of sparse tensors with fewer sense ADCs
idea: Borrow compressive sampling from MRI and radio astronomy and shrink it to the column: in non-destructive gain-cell mats holding ReLU-sparse activations, the read currents of 8 columns are summed onto one sense line through pseudo-random +/-1 select patterns, taking 3 measurements per 8 columns, and a small base-die solver reconstructs the (at most 1-of-8 nonzero) data. Dense data falls back to normal column reads.
why: Cuts sense circuitry ~2.7x and read energy per useful bit for sparse AI data (facts 7, 8); applies to the 50-90% sparse share of activation traffic.

title: Guard-driven bitline shields borrowed from femtoamp electrometers
idea: Scale the lab electrometer's driven guard down to the bitline: a 2-transistor follower in the bonded CMOS tier drives a shield trace beside each bitline to the bitline's own voltage during charge sharing, so bitline-to-neighbor and bitline-to-plate capacitance sees almost no voltage and stops soaking up signal.
why: Effective Cbl falls ~30-45%, so either Cs drops ~1.5x (fact 1) or bitlines double in length and SA stripes halve (fact 7).

title: Negative-capacitance ferroelectric gate on sense-amp input pair
idea: Scale molecule-level dipole switching up into the sense path: a thin doped-HfO2 negative-capacitance layer in the gate stack of the SA input transistors gives ~2-3x internal voltage gain on the 50-100 mV charge-shared bitline signal before the latch fires.
why: More effective signal per femtocoulomb lets Cs drop ~2x or bitlines lengthen ~2x (facts 1, 7) and relaxes SA offset sizing.

title: Size sense amps for 3.5 sigma, repair the tail by columns
idea: Time-shift the design decision to wafer test: SA input pairs are sized for 3.5-sigma Pelgrom offset instead of ~6 sigma, and the ~0.02% of SAs whose offset fails at sort are mapped out once, for the chip's years-long life, with extra spare columns.
why: Matching-device area scales with the square of the sigma target, so SA input pairs shrink ~3x, SA stripes ~25-35%, about 5-8% of die area (fact 7).

title: Sense amps that self-trim offset over months via charge trapping
idea: Time jump from nanoseconds to months: each SA input transistor carries a nitride charge-trap spacer, and whenever on-die ECC corrects an error on that SA's column a micro-pulse traps a little charge to null the offset, so offsets anneal toward zero over field life and track aging.
why: Recovers the ~10-20 mV offset budget, raising sense margin ~20-30% so Cs or tRCD can shrink (facts 1, 7) and aging margin loss is cancelled.

title: Kerf-line test periphery that dies at dicing
idea: Time-scale mismatch exploited: BIST engines, fuse programmers and test muxes are used for hours but occupy die area for years, so build them in the 60-80 um scribe streets, wired across a gapped seal ring at a low metal level, and let dicing destroy them (seal closed by post-dice passivation).
why: Recovers ~3-5% of die area spent on test/DFT periphery (fact 7), raising good die per wafer at near-zero cost.

title: Latch resolution time as free soft information for decoding
idea: Time-domain readout: because a latch resolves in ~tau*ln(V/dV), a strobe flip-flop samples each SA output a few hundred ps before the normal strobe, flags any SA not yet resolved as weak, and feeds the flags as erasures to the decoder on the base die.
why: Erasures cost half an error, so the decoder tolerates ~2x more marginal reads, letting SAs shrink or bitlines lengthen (facts 1, 7); ~10-20% sense-area cut or ~1.5x lower Cs.

title: Wafer-on-wafer memory with no PHY, DLL, or pads
idea: Scale jump from die to wafer: bond a whole DRAM wafer face-to-face onto the accelerator wafer so each mat talks to logic through sub-um bonds; there are no DQ drivers, DLLs, ESD diodes, pads or SerDes, and defective mats are bypassed by wafer-level rerouting.
why: Removes ~10-15% of die area in I/O and clocking periphery (fact 7), cuts data movement to ~0.05-0.1 pJ/bit vs 3-4 pJ/bit for HBM (fact 5), with no TSV tax (fact 6).

title: Ring-counter time-slot addressing for streaming weight mats
idea: Replace the address with time: mats dedicated to streamed AI weights use a shift-register token that walks the wordlines in fixed order, one per clock, so a row's address is simply its time slot; random access remains only at mat level and row decoders shrink to one token flop per row.
why: Row-decoder area falls ~70-80% in streaming mats (fact 7) and address energy disappears; weight-sweep workloads lose nothing.

title: Micro-LED light selects mats through the silicon backside
idea: Scale jump from datacenter optics to on-die addressing: a micro-LED array on the package lid shines 1.3 um light through thinned silicon onto Ge photodiodes at each mat's driver enable, so mat selection arrives as light and the global decoders and address buses disappear.
why: Eliminates global address wiring and part of the decoder periphery (~3-5% area, fact 7) and its switching energy; helps 3D stacks where vertical wiring is scarce.

title: Floating-diffusion charge-transfer readout for sub-femtofarad slow tier
idea: Scale-shift the image-sensor floating diffusion into DRAM and slow it down: a gated transfer transistor moves the bitline's charge onto a ~0.05 fF sense node over ~200-500 ns, giving voltage gain of ~Cbl/Cfd, which makes 0.3-0.5 fF planar cells readable as a ~1 us capacity tier.
why: No high-AR capacitor (fact 1) and fewer HAR/EUV steps (fact 4); ~2-3x bits per mask set for a capacity tier behind HBM.

title: Room-temperature nanocluster single-electron electrometer as sense element
idea: Molecule-scale jump: a sub-2 nm metal-nanocluster single-electron transistor (charging energy >10 kT) at each short bitline segment counts tens of electrons, so a cell needs only ~0.02-0.05 fF (the storage gate itself) and no capacitor.
why: Deletes the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and opens 4F2 and 3D cells (fact 2); 3-5x density if SET variability is tamed.

title: Chopper-swapped multi-decision latch averaging beneath offset
idea: Time-slice one read: the isolated SA latch fires 8 times in ~1.5 ns on the same held bitline signal, swapping its inputs on alternate decisions, and a 3-bit counter takes the majority, so fixed offset cancels and noise averages out.
why: Effective offset ~5x lower keeps reads correct at ~1/3 the signal: ~2x lower Cs or 2x longer bitlines (facts 1, 7).

title: Package-level GaN switched-capacitor rails replace on-die pumps
idea: Scale shift from die to package: VPP (~3 V) and the negative wordline bias come from a GaN switched-capacitor converter embedded in the package substrate through a dense bond/TSV grid, deleting the dozens of on-die charge pumps.
why: On-die pumps take several % of area at ~30-40% efficiency; ~90%-efficient package converters roughly halve wordline supply energy (fact 10) and free ~3-5% of die (fact 7).

title: Fleet-learned per-bank sense timing pushed by firmware
idea: Scale jump to the datacenter and to years: every module reports per-bank minimum passing tRCD/tRAS from periodic margin sweeps, the fleet models them by vendor lot, temperature and age, and firmware pushes per-bank timing tables back, re-tightening or relaxing as drift appears.
why: Typical banks carry 30-50% timing slack, so ~20-30% lower latency and activation energy fleet-wide with no new silicon (facts 7, 10).

title: Periphery wafers from U.S. legacy logic fabs
idea: Scale the fab across companies: periphery (~49% of area) is made as a separate 28-40 nm CMOS wafer at U.S. foundries on depreciated tools, only the array wafer needs a DRAM fab, and U.S. OSATs hybrid-bond the two.
why: Halves the EUV/DRAM-fab area needed per bit (facts 4, 7), adds U.S. manufacturing share within ~2 years, and uses capacity that already exists.

title: Self-assembled stochastic nanowire decoders calibrated at wafer test
idea: Molecule-to-wafer jump: block-copolymer self-assembly patterns sub-10 nm address nanowires with random doping codes instead of lithographed decoders, and at wafer test each chip learns once which code reaches which row and stores it in a small address-translation table.
why: Decoder layers without EUV (fact 4) and decoders dense enough for 4F2/3D pitch (fact 7); costs ~20% of the code space.

title: Open-source CHIPS-funded DRAM periphery IP commons
idea: Scale up from company to nation: a federally funded, silicon-proven, royalty-free library of DRAM periphery blocks (sense amps, sub-wordline drivers, pumps, PHYs) on U.S. 28 nm processes, so a new U.S. entrant only has to develop arrays.
why: Cuts entrant design time ~2-3 years and ~$0.5B of cost (capital intensity, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Decay-twin reference cells make sense thresholds age with data
idea: Time-shift the sense reference: each 64-cell segment carries a '1' twin and a '0' twin written at the same moment as the data, and the SA compares data cells against the twins' decayed midpoint, so the threshold follows real leakage and temperature and rows stay readable after ~80% charge loss. The refresh engine is deleted; the mats serve paused-session KV cache and stashed tensors idle 1-60 s.
why: Readable window grows ~100-1000x beyond 64 ms for median cells (tail cells mapped to spares), removing refresh's ~46 fJ/bit, 16-33% of idle power and 10-20% of bandwidth (fact 3).

title: Rank-order sensing of constant-weight codes needs no threshold
idea: Time jump: let charge decay for minutes, because only ordering matters; data is stored in 8-cell groups as a 4-of-8 constant-weight code (70 words, ~6 bits) and a winner-take-all sense circuit picks the four highest-charge cells. Decay shifts absolute levels but not the order until the weakest '1' meets the strongest '0', so optimizer state rewritten each training step never needs refresh.
why: Threshold-free sensing stretches usable retention ~10-100x (fact 3) for 24% capacity overhead, enough to delete refresh for data rewritten within its window.

title: Recompute-on-decay replaces refresh for training activation stashes
idea: Jump from the cell timescale to the training-job timescale: activations stashed for the backward pass get no refresh; each 64 B block carries parity plus a weak-sense flag, and any flagged block is regenerated by re-running its forward segment from the nearest checkpoint, as gradient checkpointing already does.
why: Activation stashes are ~30-60% of training memory; zero refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3) for <1% recompute, since most stashes live <1 s.

title: Leakier canary cells invalidate rows of a clean DRAM cache
idea: Time-shift retention into a cache lifetime: each row has a deliberately leakier canary cell (narrower storage node, ~5x faster decay), DRAM serves only as a clean cache over flash or NV holding inference weights, and when a read finds the canary drained the row is treated as a miss and refetched, never refreshed.
why: Deletes refresh (fact 3) and the refresh-engine periphery (fact 7); refetches stay <1% of traffic when weights are read every few seconds.

title: Token-synchronous memory: decode sweeps restore every row each token
idea: Align the workload clock with the leakage clock: LLM decode reads all dense weights and active KV each token (~20-50 ms) and every DRAM read restores its row, so the refresh engine is removed from the die; a 1-bit-per-row coverage bitmap faults if any row goes unread for one retention window, and sparse MoE experts live in an NV tier.
why: Zero refresh power and 10-20% of bandwidth returned (fact 3); refresh counters and logic leave the periphery (fact 7).

title: Ferroelectric back-gate deep-freezes idle rows' access transistors
idea: Time shift: one switching event per idle episode (minutes to hours) instead of a refresh every 64 ms. A ferroelectric back-gate under each row's access transistors is flipped when the row goes idle, raising Vt ~0.8 V so subthreshold leakage drops ~10^4-10^6 and retention reaches hours; the next access flips it back, and no refresh exists.
why: Kills the leakage tail that forces refresh (fact 3) without a new storage element; ~1 FE cycle per idle episode makes ~10^10 endurance ample.

title: Per-bank TTL timers replace the refresh scheduler
idea: Swap the 64 ms refresh clock for allocation lifetimes: host allocations carry a time-to-live, each bank's periphery holds a countdown timer instead of refresh counters, and on expiry the bank's data is declared dead and the bank power-gated; TTLs are capped below the bank's certified retention.
why: Zero refresh power and simpler periphery (facts 3, 7); fits network buffers, KV caches and step-scoped tensors that make up most AI memory traffic.

title: 77 K drawer in each rack holds long-lived data refresh-free
idea: Scale jump to rack infrastructure: one liquid-nitrogen-cooled drawer per rack hosts DRAM whose leakage at 77 K gives hours-to-days retention, with sense amps re-centered for cryogenic Vt and lower offset; warm DRAM keeps hot data while the cold drawer holds embedding tables and long-lived state with refresh disabled.
why: Zero refresh power (fact 3) and faster cryo periphery; the ~10 W-per-W cooling overhead restricts it to capacity-heavy, low-access data.

title: Gallium-oxide access-transistor arrays bonded onto silicon periphery
idea: Material jump with a time jump to years of retention: 4.8 eV-gap beta-Ga2O3 transistors, grown on native substrates and layer-transferred, form the cell array with off-currents below 10^-21 A, and the slower array is read through time-domain integrating sense amps on a bonded Si CMOS wafer; no refresh circuitry is built.
why: Retention beyond product life means zero refresh (fact 3) while fast Si periphery is kept; a crystalline wide-gap route distinct from IGZO.

title: NEMS contact-switch access device with true zero off-current
idea: Scale jump from MEMS relays to ~20 nm: the access transistor is replaced by a nano-electromechanical contact switch with a vacuum gap when off, so the storage node leaks only through the capacitor dielectric and surfaces, giving hours of retention; refresh is omitted and data idle longer moves to NV.
why: Removes the subthreshold/GIDL leakage tail (fact 3) entirely -> zero refresh; contact wear and ~ns pull-in are the risks.

title: Log-domain time-to-threshold sensing keeps decayed gain cells readable
idea: Time-domain sensing: gain cells are read by timing how long the read current takes to discharge a sense node, decided on a log-time scale; since subthreshold read current is exponential in stored voltage, a '1' that has lost 0.6 V still discharges ~10^3x faster than a '0', so cells stay readable 3-10x longer, reaching minutes, and session KV caches need no refresh.
why: Stretches gain-cell retention past session idle times, deleting refresh (fact 3); the log scale also absorbs temperature drift.

title: One-shot ferroelectric shadow freezes rows before charge leaks
idea: Time-shift between two storage physics: the capacitor stack has a thin HZO layer left untouched during DRAM-speed use, and when a row's age counter passes ~half its retention one pulse copies the charge state into polarization, after which charge may leak freely; the next read senses polarization switching current and returns the row to charge mode.
why: No periodic refresh (fact 3), and FE endurance is spent only once per long idle episode, sidestepping FeRAM's endurance limit.

title: Coulomb-blockade nanocrystal storage islands read by gain FETs
idea: Molecule-scale jump: 5-20 electrons are stored on a ~3 nm Si or metal nanocrystal between thin tunnel barriers, where charging energy >> kT blocks leakage, and read non-destructively through the threshold shift of an adjacent gain FET; writes use low-field direct tunneling that does not wear the oxide, and no refresh is issued.
why: Retention of ~10^3-10^5 s at nanocapacitor size means zero refresh (fact 3) and no capacitor (fact 1).

title: Decay-as-weight-decay memory for training master weights
idea: Time-shift the meaning of leakage: master weights and optimizer moments are rewritten every training step (~1 s), so they sit in refresh-free DRAM where MSBs use double-size robust cells and low mantissa bits use tiny cells whose 1->0 decay acts as stochastic rounding toward zero, a built-in weight decay.
why: Zero refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3) and ~30% more bits per area for low-order bits (fact 1).

title: Sell DRAM by the perishable byte-second
idea: Datacenter-scale business model: memory is priced per byte-second of guaranteed retention; 'perishable' refresh-free SKUs ship with no refresh engine and a certified 10 s window at a 30-40% discount, and tenants pay a premium only for data that must outlive it, served from NV tiers.
why: Zero refresh power across the perishable fleet (fact 3), smaller periphery and better binning yield; gives customers a reason to annotate data lifetimes.

title: Model-ROM DIMMs hold frozen weights with DRAM interfaces
idea: Time jump to model-release cadence: inference weights frozen for months are written once into via- or antifuse-programmed ROM mats that reuse DRAM-style sense amps and the DDR/LPDDR interface, and modules are recycled when the model retires.
why: Weights are ~60-80% of inference memory; capacitor-free ~4F2 ROM cells need zero refresh (fact 3), give ~3x density (fact 1) and skip capacitor EUV/HAR steps (fact 4).

title: Retention-class mats exposed as address bits
idea: Use test time as a time machine: at wafer test, hours-long 85 C dwells measure each mat's worst cell, tail cells are remapped to spare rows, and mats are binned into retention classes (0.1, 1, 10, 100 s) that the decoder exposes as high address bits; the allocator places each object only in a class longer than its maximum idle time, and refresh is never issued.
why: Zero refresh (fact 3) with no new materials, since median mats already hold data for seconds; retention variation becomes a product feature.

title: JEDEC refresh-free mode with certified retention window
idea: Scale jump to the industry: a JEDEC mode-register bit disables refresh entirely and advertises a vendor-certified retention window (for example 2 s at 85 C) proven at qualification, and OSes and AI runtimes get a standard malloc_ttl API to place only data whose idle time fits.
why: Makes zero refresh deployable fleet-wide (fact 3) and lets vendors drop refresh logic from periphery (fact 7).

title: Leak-to-archive cells write their own nonvolatile backup
idea: Time-shift the leak into a write: each cell's leakage path runs through a tiny ionic memristive integrator, so the charge draining from a stored '1' over seconds moves ions and leaves a resistance state recording it; after full decay the sense amp reads the memristor instead, and the next write resets it.
why: The leaking energy itself writes the backup, so refresh power is zero (fact 3); memristor reset endurance is the main risk.

title: Thermally isolated array tier cooled by microfluidics
idea: Scale-shift the thermal stack: the array wafer bonds to the hot periphery/logic wafer through sparse Cu pillars across a vacuum gap and is cooled from its own backside by microfluidic channels on 10 C rack chilled water, holding cells ~75 C below the logic; with leakage halving every ~10 C, worst-case retention goes from 64 ms to ~10 s and refresh is dropped for step- and token-scoped data.
why: ~150-200x retention deletes refresh (fact 3) and fixes heat-driven retention loss in memory-on-logic stacks.

title: FD-SOI back-biased hold mode for idle mats
idea: Time jump between ns access mode and minute-scale hold mode: access transistors sit on fully depleted SOI, so there is no storage-junction leakage to substrate, and the periphery switches an idle mat's buried back plane to -2 V (a held voltage, no current), suppressing subthreshold leakage ~10^3-10^4 so data idle for minutes survives with no refresh.
why: Removes junction and subthreshold leakage paths (fact 3) -> zero refresh for data idle under minutes; static back bias draws no refresh power.

title: Polyoxometalate redox clusters as molecular gain-cell storage nodes
idea: Molecule-scale jump: a monolayer of polyoxometalate clusters, which hold discrete electrons in deep molecular orbitals, forms the storage layer in the gate stack of a gain FET; writes add or remove 1-2 electrons per cluster at low voltage and the deep levels keep the charge for hours, so no refresh is scheduled.
why: Hours of retention -> zero refresh (fact 3), no capacitor (fact 1), and self-assembly instead of EUV patterning (fact 4).

title: Van der Waals resonant-tunneling pairs make each node bistable
idea: Atomic-layer scale jump: two stacked graphene/hBN resonant-tunneling diodes on each storage node form a Goto pair, so the node latches statically at either rail with valley current engineered below 1 fA; data never decays, so there is no refresh cycle at all.
why: Zero refresh power and bandwidth (fact 3), with hold current below the ~1 fA refresh-equivalent; scaling the vdW RTD peak-to-valley ratio is the risk.
